claims.text: The FA*IR algorithm produces a top-k fair ranking from n candidates in O(n + k log k) time complexity.
FA*IR achieves higher or equal ordering utility compared to the baseline method by Feldman et al. across all evaluated dataset conditions.
On the COMPAS recidivism dataset with African-American candidates as the protected group at p=0.5, FA*IR achieves an NDCG of 0.9858 and an ordering utility loss of 0.2026.
Algorithm 1 iteratively computes the significance level adjustment to account for multiple prefix hypothesis tests in O(k^2) time.

evidence.description: FA*IR has running time O(n + k log k); which includes building the two O(k) size priority queues from n items and processing them to obtain the ranking.
Third, FA*IR achieves higher or equal ordering utility in all conditions.
Table 6 reports NDCG 0.9858 and ordering utility loss 0.2026 for FA*IR on dataset D1 (COMPAS, race=Afr.-Am., p=0.5), compared to NDCG 0.9779 and ordering utility loss 0.2281 for Feldman et al.
Algorithm 1 maintains vector S across iterations to yield the rejection probability of a fair ranking in O(k^2) running time.

methodologies.name: FA*IR
methodologies.description: A post-processing fair top-k ranking algorithm that greedily selects candidates from priority queues to maximize utility while guaranteeing statistical ranked group fairness across all list prefixes.

limitations.text: The model makes the simplifying assumption that there is a single dominant legally-protected attribute of interest.
If there are fewer than k protected candidates available in the input pool, the tail of the output ranking may fail to satisfy the ranked group fairness constraint.
Machine learning ranking models trained on datasets incorporating preexisting bias will embody and reinforce that bias in their outputs.

future_work.text: Extending the ranked group fairness framework to deal with multiple protected attributes simultaneously.
Developing in-processing fair ranking algorithms rather than post-processing methods.
Measuring algorithm robustness to noise in qualification scores and evaluating real-world application impact.
